name: Maroon
lede: Maroon is a dark brownish red, named from the French word for the chestnut, and it began as a brown before it became a red.

sections.title: A chestnut, then a red
sections.body: Paterson derives *maroon* from French *marron*, chestnut, and adds that the French word may in turn come from a Hebrew word for chestnut, a guess he marks with a *perhaps* [1]. St Clair's glossary says the color was originally nut brown and now means a brownish dark red [2]. The chestnut stayed where it was, and the word moved toward red. Our date data has the first English use of *maroon* as a color word in 1789 [3].

sections.title: Which maroon
sections.body:
The swatch, #800000, is the web keyword for maroon [1]. Paterson lists it among the X11 colors and among the 16 basic color names of early web design [1][4]. It is a pure dark red with no brown in it, and ISCC-NBS, which names colors by looking, calls it a strong reddish brown, about five units away [3].

Older sources mean something browner. Ridgway's 1912 Maroon, carried into ISCC-NBS, sits near #5B3B34, taken from a scan of an aged plate and so approximate [3]. The xkcd color survey's maroon is a deep crimson, #650021 [3]. Sources also disagree about X11: Paterson gives its Maroon as #800000, while our library carries a separate Maroon (X11) at the pinker #B03060 [1][3]. On screens the word names a neighborhood, not a point.

sections.title: A respectable red
sections.body: In the early 1850s, English fashion manuals condemned scarlet and crimson as vulgar but allowed a lady dark reds, brick reds and maroon, especially a married one [5]. The vogue for dark reds, together with the full crinoline skirt that swallowed yards of cloth, helped revive the cochineal trade [5]. Greenfield adds that some women who dressed in public only in dull maroon wore bright red woolen petticoats beneath it [5].

sections.title: Maroons from the factory
sections.body:
Many maroon pigments come from modern chemistry. In cadmium red, a cadmium sulfide-selenide, more selenium moves the color from orange toward dark maroon [6]. The Pigment Compendium gives selenium-to-cadmium ratios of 10:90 for orange, 20:80 for bright red and 30:70 for dark maroon [7]. Ball says the compound now called cadmium red was not available commercially until 1910, and Bayer made it more reliably in 1919 [6].

The cadmium mercury sulfides run from orange to maroon as the mercury sulfide share rises from 11 to 26 per cent, and are said to have been developed after a shortage of selenium in the later 1940s [7]. Organic chemists reached maroon too. Benzimidazolone pigments give maroons as well as yellows and oranges, and lithol maroon is a barium lithol red bound with rosin, from the lithol red discovered by P. Julius in 1899 [8]. Perylene pigments were found in 1912 and 1913 but came into general use only after 1950, and perylene maroon is listed among artists' pigments [8].

sections.title: Maroon in paint
sections.body: Ball notes that Rothko, wary of letting viewers enjoy his canvases as decoration, toned down his bright early palette for blacks, browns, greys and deep maroons [9]. In the Rothko Chapel murals of 1965, whose dark maroon monochromes are marred by whitish streaks and cracking, the synthetic alizarin-based reds have kept their intensity [9].

sections.title: Why maroon is a relative color
sections.body: A hue needs only two numbers, and a name like maroon needs a third. Livingstone points out that maroon and pink are the same hue and differ only in luminance, and that maroon is red light surrounded by something lighter [10]. Gurney uses Munsell notation to make the point: a maroon can be written R 3/6, a hue, a value of 3 out of 10 and a chroma of 6 [11]. Our swatch is 0.5YR 2.5/11.2 in the same system, darker and far stronger than that example [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Maroon appears in 292 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 1.23 per cent, and in 236 counted by lightness rank inside each painting [12]. It is more common than 73 per cent of the named colors, and plays an accent in 82 per cent of those 236 [12]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 3.8 per cent of the 945 paintings from that century, 3.4 times the baseline of the same museums [12]. [[painter:sandro-botticelli|Botticelli]] has it in 4 of his 48 works here, but no painter stands out against the baseline [12]. It travels with [[black-bean]] and [[chinese-red]] (lift 10.0 and 6.9) [12].

The nearest cut stone in our gem data is [[gem:coral|coral]], a rare deep ox-blood red, at 2.4 units, then [[gem:cinnabar|cinnabar]] at 3.5 [13]. Close look-alikes are [[blood-red]], [[falu-red]] and [[deep-red]] [13]. In our film notes the nearest color is the restaurant red of [[film:vertigo|Vertigo]] (1958), 5.3 units away [13]. In printed English the word peaks in the 2010s and rose fastest in the 2000s [12].

The earliest archive match is a work of about 1290 in the Rijksmuseum, 499 years before the name's first record [12]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [12].

questions.q: What does the French word marron, the source of maroon, mean?
In cadmium red, which change moves the color from orange toward dark maroon?
True or false: maroon and pink differ in hue.

openers: Maroon began as nut brown: the word is French for chestnut.
Maroon is red light surrounded by something lighter, and pink is the same hue with more luminance.
The web maroon, #800000, has no brown in it, while older maroons did.

issues: Softened "most maroon pigments are twentieth-century chemistry" (lithol red is 1899)
